title: Nvidia's Cloud Partnership Ties Prompt Skepticism Over New Chinese Rental Restrictions
summary:
The world's largest AI chip designer is facing criticism over whether it can realistically police its supply chain to stop foreign labs from utilizing high-end hardware. Despite public efforts to curb Chinese access to its technology, Nvidia continues to list Megaspeed—a company currently under federal investigation—as a cloud partner on its website. Critics also point to Nvidia's relationship with Aivres, a U.S. subsidiary of the entity-listed Chinese firm Inspur, which has reportedly supplied chips to companies that provide server access to Chinese state-owned enterprises.

These concerns follow reports that Nvidia verbally instructed its data center and cloud clients since the summer to ensure no more than 49% of their compute services are sold to Chinese customers. The mandate, which applies to new contracts, is intended to close a remote access loophole that allows Chinese firms to rent GPU capacity when they cannot legally import chips under U.S. export controls. To enforce the rule, Nvidia has requested that partners disclose the identities of their end users, a move that comes as the market for AI hardware in China has surged; B300 racks have sold for $2.54M in China last month, compared to roughly $600,000 in international markets.

selectedTweets.text:
Nvidia is now requiring data centers to not sell more than 49% of their compute to Chinese customers. But in what world is selling 49% of the world's most valuable resource to China a "win" for America? The number should be 0%; if Chinese firms can't buy a chip due to export controls they also shouldn't be permitted to rent access to it. 

The fact that this remote access loophole exists--and that Nvidia even felt compelled to announce this new policy because it undoubtedly has so many customers currently renting 100% of their compute to China--just shows how badly export controls are being mismanaged.

The timing of this story—on the eve of the midterms—suggests NVIDIA thinks the balance on export controls is shifting and sees self-regulation as its best option.

But is anyone going to trust NVIDIA to self-regulate? NVIDIA still lists Megaspeed as a cloud partner on its website. That’s right, Megaspeed, a company under federal investigation and whose former executive is a Chinese intelligence asset! Still an NVIDIA partner! 

This is not a company that takes national security seriously.

selectedTweets.text:
Nvidia also has partnered with Aivres, the US subsidiary of Entity-Listed Chinese company Inspur. 

Aivres is a "trusted server partner" that has supplied chips to Megaspeed, which sells remote access to China. Aivres' chips and parts have also flowed through to Maginfra, a Chinese company that sells servers to state-owned enterprises.

The 49% rule by Nvidia would have been welcomed if they had a demonstrated track record of being serious about due diligence. But unfortunately the evidence of this is very thin.
